segment_name: A Woman Wagering with Fate: Gwendolen's Entrance

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that's been stuck in my head — that Gwendolen is one of the great comic characters in English literature, right up until the moment she isn't. Can you walk us into that opening casino scene and show us what you mean? Because most people's memory of this novel is tragedy, not comedy.
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read or closely paraphrase the opening casino passage and establish the magnetic, funny Gwendolen before the other panelists complicate it — sets up the 'confidence of ignorance' observation as a gut-punch rather than a thesis

questions.question: Eleanor, you described the narration in this opening as 'architecture' — which I love. But I want to push on that. When Eliot's describing Gwendolen at the gaming table, are we actually inside her head, or are we being kept just slightly outside it? Because that feels like it matters enormously for how we judge her.
questions.intent: Get Hartley to demonstrate the free indirect discourse technique using the specific passage about Gwendolen's experience at the tables — make the formal argument vivid and audible, not academic

questions.question: James, I have a feeling you want to flip this entire conversation on its head. Eleanor and Caroline are both talking about what Eliot does to Gwendolen on the page — but you want to talk about what the law was doing to Gwendolen before she ever walked into that casino, right?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone's strongest institutional argument — that the gambling is rational, not pathological — and set up a direct collision with Hartley's formalist reading and Woodcourt's tragic-comic frame

questions.question: Eleanor, James is basically saying: stop looking at the sentences, look at the system. Does the formal genius you're describing actually let Eliot off the hook from making a political argument? Or is the form *the* political argument?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Hartley's formalism and Blackstone's institutional critique — get Hartley to either defend or absorb the legal-historical reading into her narrative framework

questions.question: Caroline, here's the question I keep circling back to. All three of you are defending Gwendolen in different ways — James says the system is the villain, Eleanor says the narration keeps us from judging her, and you're saying she's genuinely intelligent and even funny. But Eliot does condemn her, at least a little, doesn't she? Or are we all just refusing to let her be flawed?
questions.intent: Create a moment of productive tension by suggesting all three experts are too sympathetic — push toward whether Gwendolen's own choices carry any moral weight, or whether the novel fully displaces blame onto external forces

steering_notes: This segment should move from close reading (get the prose on the table early via Woodcourt) into formal analysis (Hartley) into structural-historical argument (Blackstone) and then circle back to a genuine disagreement about moral accountability. Don't let it become a seminar — keep asking 'but what does the sentence actually say?' to ground abstract arguments. The comic-to-tragic frame is the emotional thread: use it to open and close the segment. If Blackstone and Hartley get into it about form vs. system, let it breathe — that's the best radio in this group.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that modern readers 'pathologize' Gwendolen directly challenges Hartley's reading of free indirect discourse as structuring moral ambiguity — Hartley should be asked whether her formalist sympathy is itself a form of pathologizing dressed up as aesthetics

Woodcourt and Hartley both emphasize Eliot's prose rhythm and sentence structure as doing moral work, but for different ends — Woodcourt hears complicity and tragedy, Hartley hears formal self-consciousness about narrative itself; push them to name specifically what they think the prose is *for*

Blackstone's legal-historical frame and Woodcourt's 'intelligent woman with no real options' argument are actually close allies, but they should be made to discover that on air rather than having it pointed out — ask each of them separately whether intelligence without legal recourse is the same as freedom

segment_name: The Weight of Belonging: Deronda's Question

questions.question: Eleanor, you made this claim in our chat that stopped me cold — you said Deronda is less a character than a *structural device*, that his lack of fixed identity is basically load-bearing for the whole novel. But doesn't that risk turning him into a kind of vacuum? What's actually *in* Daniel Deronda?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to articulate her formal/modernist thesis strongly and early, and set up the tension with Caroline's view that he's a psychologically real portrait of passivity

questions.question: Caroline, you said something that I keep coming back to — that Deronda doesn't *discover* his identity, he's *told* it, and he just... accepts. There's a passage you wanted to read about his 'possible self' and how uncertainty becomes a kind of prison. Can you take us there? Because I want to hear whether you think that's Eliot being sympathetic to him or quietly devastating him.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the 'possible self' passage and land her core thesis about Deronda as sleepwalker — the word 'devastating' should provoke Eleanor and James

questions.question: James, I have to give you a chance to push back on both of them, because your read feels almost like a different novel. You're saying this isn't really a psychological portrait at all — it's about institutions, inheritance laws, community obligations. So when Caroline says Deronda is 'imprisoned' by being claimed, and Eleanor says he's a formal experiment in selflessness — are they both missing the thing Eliot is actually anatomizing?
questions.intent: Provoke a three-way disagreement by letting James articulate the legal-institutional reading as a corrective — get him to name the specific machinery of inheritance and community obligation Eliot grounds this in

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something that I think James will have strong feelings about — that Deronda's displacement is *prior to* and maybe independent of his Jewish genealogy. But James, and maybe Caroline too: isn't that exactly the move the novel refuses to let us make? Can you actually separate the psychological experience of not-belonging from the specific historical and legal situation of Jewish identity in Victorian England?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Eleanor's formalist reading and James's historically grounded one — this is the segment's central disagreement and needs airtime

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Caroline, you said the most unsettling thing might be that embracing his heritage doesn't free Deronda — it just gives his imprisonment a name. James, you'd probably say that's not imprisonment, that's what *belonging to any real community* actually feels like. And Eleanor, you'd say he's still performing his destiny at the end rather than living it. So: does this novel have a way out for him, or is Eliot deliberately sealing every door?
questions.intent: Force a closing synthesis where all three positions collide — the question is genuinely open and each expert should feel their reading is at stake

steering_notes: This segment risks getting too abstract too fast — keep pulling experts back to specific passages and specific moments in the text. Caroline is the best anchor here because she reads closely and emotionally; use her to slow James down when he goes macro-historical and to give Eleanor's formal claims a human face. The key tension to cultivate is Eleanor vs James: formalist withholding vs institutional materiality. Caroline sits interestingly between them — psychological and close-reading but resistant to both pure form and pure history. Don't let the Jewish identity question become the *only* lens too early; let James bring it in as a corrective after the psychological readings have had room. The segment should feel like it's building toward an unanswerable question about freedom and constraint — that's the productive place to land.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline says Deronda is 'told' his identity and accepts it — Eleanor would say that's a formal choice by Eliot, not just a character trait; James would say it reflects the actual mechanics of how communities claim members. All three readings of the same moment should collide.

Eleanor's claim that Deronda's displacement is prior to and independent of his genealogy directly contradicts James's insistence that you cannot separate psychological belonging from its legal and historical scaffolding — this needs explicit airtime.

James's point that belonging means accepting community rules you didn't make and can't fully control is actually a darker version of Caroline's 'imprisonment' thesis — they may agree more than they realize, and surfacing that unexpected alignment could be the segment's best moment.

segment_name: Drawing Rooms and Social Cages: Victorian Women's Constraint

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that I keep thinking about — that Eliot doesn't liberate her women through plot, she liberates them through consciousness. Can you show us what you mean? Is there a passage where you can actually hear that happening in the prose itself?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to demonstrate the craft argument with a specific close reading — her strongest take, performed rather than explained. Sets up the space/interiority tension for the whole segment.

questions.question: James, I want to push on something. Eleanor's just described Eliot's prose as a kind of liberation — consciousness expanding even as the body is trapped. You'd say that's... what, exactly? A consolation prize?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone to make his 'engineered helplessness' argument in direct response to Hartley's aesthetic case — forces the material vs. formal disagreement into the open without framing it as an academic debate.

questions.question: Caroline, both Eleanor and James are circling around the question of whether Gwendolen knows what's happening to her. You said she's aware of the cage but can't articulate the way out. Is there a moment in the text where you can actually feel that gap — where she sees it but can't say it?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to quote or describe a specific Gwendolen passage — ideally the Grandcourt attention scene — and introduce the psychological internalization argument that she wants to push against both the formal and materialist readings.

questions.question: James, Caroline used the word 'choice' about Gwendolen marrying Grandcourt and then basically took it back — said it's not really choice when all the options are terrible. But you'd go further than that, wouldn't you? You'd say the legal architecture means the word 'choice' is almost dishonest here.
questions.intent: Set up the disagreement between Blackstone's structural argument and Woodcourt's psychological one — Woodcourt thinks women police themselves, Blackstone thinks the system does it for them. Gets both in the room at once.

questions.question: Here's the one thing I want to put to all three of you: is Eliot *in* this problem? Caroline flagged that sometimes the philosophical remove in the narration keeps us at a distance from the women's actual suffering. Is the novel's formal sophistication — the thing Eleanor is celebrating — also part of what keeps us watching from the outside?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision — Hartley has to defend the formal sophistication she admires, Woodcourt can press the 'don't let Eliot off the hook' point, and Blackstone can argue none of it matters if the structural critique is blunted. High energy, no easy landing.

steering_notes: The natural fault line here is material vs. formal vs. psychological — Blackstone wants to talk about law and economics, Hartley wants to talk about prose architecture, Woodcourt wants to talk about internalized performance. Let all three frameworks get air early, then push them to argue with each other rather than past each other. The best radio moment will be when Hartley's 'liberation through consciousness' argument meets Woodcourt's 'don't let Eliot off the hook' — those two are superficially compatible but actually quite different about what the novel is *for*. Watch for Blackstone to dismiss aesthetic arguments as beside the point; let Hartley respond to that directly. End on the meta-question about Eliot's own remove — that's the one that should leave listeners arguing after the episode.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that Eliot 'liberates through consciousness' directly challenges Woodcourt's worry that the novel's philosophical remove keeps us from feeling women's suffering as suffering — not just observing it. Get Woodcourt to name that tension explicitly.

Blackstone's insistence that 'choice' is almost meaningless within the legal architecture sits in productive tension with Woodcourt's more psychological account of self-policing — they agree on the conclusion but for reasons that actually conflict. Surface that.

Woodcourt's point that you need to read Eliot aloud to feel the claustrophobia from inside is a practical test of Hartley's formal argument — if Hartley agrees, ask them to demonstrate it together with a passage. That's a strong radio moment.

segment_name: Tyranny in Silence: Reading Grandcourt's Control

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our conversation that I keep coming back to — that Grandcourt is the only character whose presence actually *changes the sentence structure around him*. That's a wild claim. Can you show us what you mean? Like, give us the prose on the page.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read aloud and demonstrate her formal argument — anchors the whole segment in close reading and sets up the contrast between form-focused and content-focused readings

questions.question: Caroline, you've said this is one of the cruelest love stories ever written — but Grandcourt never shouts, never hits, barely speaks. How does Eliot make cruelty feel *physical* when the weapon is basically just a man being very quiet in a room?
questions.intent: Draw out Caroline's strongest take on silence as violence, get her to read the cutting dialogue moments, and implicitly set up James's challenge that the real weapon isn't silence but law

questions.question: James, I want to push on something. Eleanor and Caroline are both describing Grandcourt as this almost supernatural force — the silence, the prose rhythm, the psychological horror. And you're basically saying: no, he's just a man with a marriage certificate and a very good lawyer. Does the legal argument risk making him *less* frightening, not more?
questions.intent: Provoke productive disagreement — force James to defend the material reading against the more visceral formal and psychological readings, and get him to name the specific legal mechanisms Eliot is documenting

questions.question: Eleanor, you said Eliot *refuses* Grandcourt psychological depth — that he has no interiority. But James is saying the law already gave him everything he needs; he doesn't require depth. Are you two actually agreeing about his emptiness but for completely different reasons? Or is there a real fight here?
questions.intent: Surface the tension between the formal reading and the materialist reading — both see Grandcourt as a structural force but mean completely different things by that; push them to either find common ground or sharpen their disagreement

questions.question: Caroline, you said readers who find this novel slow are missing the psychological horror happening sentence by sentence. But here's the devil's advocate position: if the tyranny is so effectively embedded in the prose rhythm, does that make the novel almost *too* uncomfortable to read — and is that a feature or a problem?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to articulate why the discomfort is the point, potentially draw out Eleanor on Eliot's modernist experiment, and let James connect it to why the novel's reception was cooler than Middlemarch

steering_notes: Open with Eleanor's formal claim because it's the most surprising and requires demonstration — it immediately grounds the segment in actual prose rather than theme-talk. The central tension to cultivate is between Eleanor's formal reading, Caroline's experiential-emotional reading, and James's materialist-legal reading. They're not actually incompatible, but they feel like they're competing, and that productive friction is the engine of the segment. Push James to be specific about legal mechanisms when he goes abstract. Pull Eleanor back to the body of the text if she drifts into theory. Keep asking Caroline to read aloud — her instinct to perform the prose is the best radio in the room. End on James's provocation about who Grandcourt has become in the modern economy — that's the note that sends listeners out thinking.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor says Grandcourt has no interiority — a formal choice; James says he needs no interiority because the law provides his power — these positions rhyme suspiciously and should be put directly to both of them together

Caroline wants to read Gwendolen's will and spirit being systematically unmade; Eleanor wants to show agency dissolving in the prose itself — this is either the same argument in different registers or a genuine disagreement about whether Gwendolen retains subjectivity at all, and that's worth surfacing

James's claim that Eliot is documenting injustice that didn't end in 1876 sits in tension with Eleanor's claim that this is a formally radical, almost modernist novel — one wants to historicize, the other wants to aestheticize, and Caroline is likely to side with Eleanor here which makes it 2-v-1

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that I can't stop thinking about — that wit is actually *how* people deceive themselves, not the opposite of it. Can you find us a passage where you can actually hear that happening? Like, where the character's cleverness is doing the covering-up work?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read and anatomize a specific passage, demonstrating the free indirect discourse point and the sentence-level craftsmanship. Sets up the core tension of the segment.

questions.question: James, I can hear you already wanting to interrupt — because your argument is that what Eleanor's calling a *psychological* mechanism is actually something colder and more structural. You used the word 'forensic.' What do you mean by that? Eliot's angrier than she looks?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's sharpest take — that Eliot's comedy is a form of institutional indictment, not just psychological insight. Provokes direct disagreement with Hartley's reading of wit as compassionate anatomy.

questions.question: Caroline, you're both making Eliot sound quite severe — James sees prosecution, Eleanor sees dissection. But you talked about *tenderness*. Is it possible to be that tender and that brutal at the same time? Pick a moment with Gwendolen, or even Deronda himself — because you made this point that Deronda becomes almost ridiculous when seen through other people's eyes, and I want to know what that looks like on the page.
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read a passage involving Deronda-as-projection, which sets up her argument about romantic fantasy and mirrors Blackstone and Hartley's structural vs. psychological debate with a third option: comic tragedy.

questions.question: James, here's a provocation. You said some of these characters *fail upward* — they have the luxury of self-deception because money and law protect them. But who are you thinking of specifically? Because Caroline would say that's still a tragic portrait, and Eleanor would say Eliot makes us *complicit* in their delusion. So whose side is Eliot actually on when she's being funny about someone like Grandcourt?
questions.intent: Force a concrete example that will either confirm Blackstone's forensic reading or complicate it — and create a three-way disagreement about what Eliot's comic tone is actually *doing* morally.

questions.question: Last one — and I want everyone in on this. Eleanor, you said the second time you read this novel the comedy and the tragedy hit you simultaneously. What does that actually feel like as a reader? And I want to know whether James thinks that double effect is Eliot being generous, or whether it's the most devastating version of the indictment. Is the heartbreak the point, or is it a way of letting us — and the characters — off the hook?
questions.intent: Close the segment by bringing all three into direct conversation about the novel's ultimate tonal and moral stance — generous or prosecutorial, tragic or comic, forgiving or indicting. Forces a genuine three-way disagreement about what the reader is left with.

steering_notes: The central fault line is between Hartley's psychological-formalist reading (wit as self-deception mechanism, complicity through free indirect discourse) and Blackstone's institutional-forensic reading (wit as indictment of systems that protect folly). Woodcourt is the swing voice — she's more interested in the emotional texture and the tragic-comic double effect, which could align with either or cut across both. Push for concrete passages early; the segment dies if it stays abstract. The Deronda-as-projection point is an underexplored comic seam — press Woodcourt on it if energy dips. Blackstone's gender point (women's folly punished, men's folly merely colorful) has not been directly asked about and could be a late-segment grenade if needed.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley says wit is compassionate anatomy; Blackstone says it's forensic indictment — these are direct contradictions about Eliot's emotional stance toward her characters. Get them to name the same passage and interpret it differently.

Woodcourt says Deronda becomes 'almost ridiculous' through others' projections; Hartley says the novel's moral seriousness is load-bearing. This is a direct tension about whether we're supposed to take Deronda seriously at all — push both on it simultaneously.

Blackstone's 'fail upward' argument (structural privilege enables self-deception) vs. Woodcourt's 'tenderness' argument (self-deception feels inevitable and necessary) — these aren't quite contradictory but they imply very different readers. One sees a cold social machine; one sees a human tragedy. Make them argue about which Eliot wrote.

All three have implicit disagreements about what re-reading does — Woodcourt says the second reading breaks your heart; Hartley says the form traps us on first read; Blackstone implies re-reading just confirms the indictment. Good closing thread.

segment_name: The Architecture of Conscience: Moral Awakening as Plot

questions.question: Caroline, let's open with something concrete. You said in our chat that Eliot actually *writes* conscience into the sentence structure — that the prose itself forces a reckoning. Can you pick a specific moment, read a bit of it if you have it, and show us what you mean? Like, what is the sentence actually *doing*?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to model close reading immediately, establish the prose-as-conscience argument early, and set up Hartley to agree but push further and Blackstone to push back

questions.question: Eleanor, you'd agree the syntax is doing moral work — but you used this phrase in our conversation that stuck with me: you said conscience in this novel is a *condition* Eliot keeps *reopening*, not a destination the plot arrives at. What does that mean for how we read, say, Gwendolen? Does she ever actually *get* anywhere morally, or is Eliot just keeping her suspended?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's strongest take on irresolution vs. arrival, and directly provoke Woodcourt whose pre-interview leaned toward moral vindication and earned complexity

questions.question: James, I want to bring you in here because I suspect you think both Eleanor and Caroline are missing something — they're both talking about prose style, sentence rhythms, psychological suspension. But your argument is that Deronda's conscience doesn't awaken in some purely interior space. It awakens when he runs smack into what the *law* has done to his identity. Can you make that case? Where does the legal architecture enter the moral one?
questions.intent: Let Blackstone land his materialist critique of the psychological reading, introduce the inheritance and legal exclusion argument, and create direct tension with Hartley and Woodcourt

questions.question: Eleanor, here's where I want to push on you a bit. You said Eliot's real innovation is dramatizing the *narrative we tell ourselves to avoid answering* the moral question. James is saying the legal system tells that narrative *for* Deronda — it erases his origins before he even gets a chance to evade them. Are those two arguments actually in conflict, or is Eliot doing both things at once?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement between Hartley's grammar-of-evasion argument and Blackstone's institutional-erasure argument — find out if they can be reconciled or if this is a genuine disagreement about where the novel locates moral agency

questions.question: Last one — and I'll open this to everyone. Caroline, you said something that I keep coming back to: that most Victorian novels *punish* women for mixed feelings, and Eliot *vindicates* the complexity of conscience instead. But James might say that vindication is cold comfort if the institutions don't change. And Eleanor might say there's no vindication at all — just permanent irresolution. So: does this novel end with anything you'd call moral hope, or is that a category Eliot doesn't believe in?
questions.intent: Force all three experts to declare a position on the novel's moral conclusion — create triangulated disagreement and give the segment a strong closing argument rather than a trailing-off

steering_notes: This segment has strong natural tension built in: Hartley and Woodcourt share a commitment to prose-as-moral-argument but diverge on whether conscience resolves or stays permanently open; Blackstone is the odd one out who thinks both are too interior. Keep pulling Blackstone back in whenever the conversation goes purely stylistic — his job is to remind everyone that syntax doesn't survive a marriage contract. The key dramatic question is whether the three positions are reconcilable or whether they represent genuinely different novels. Push toward that question in the back half. Don't let the segment become a seminar on free indirect discourse — keep asking 'but what does this mean for how we *feel* about these characters at the end?'
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's 'grammar of evasion' argument vs. Blackstone's 'institutional erasure' argument — Deronda can't evade what was hidden from him by law, so who or what is doing the evading? This is the sharpest disagreement in the room and should be named explicitly.

Woodcourt's claim that Eliot 'vindicates' moral complexity directly contradicts Hartley's claim that Eliot offers no resolution — both are optimistic about Eliot but for opposite reasons. Worth surfacing: is vindicating complexity the same as endorsing irresolution?

Blackstone's line that 'individual conscience without institutional reform is nearly useless' is a direct challenge to both other experts' frameworks, neither of which engages seriously with material conditions. Let him say this clearly and then let Woodcourt and Hartley respond — they'll both push back but from different angles.

segment_name: The Unfinished Self: Identity, Art, and Meaning

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started that reading Daniel Deronda aloud is basically mandatory — that you can't understand what Eliot's doing unless you hear it. Can you pick a moment, a specific passage, where Gwendolen or Deronda is mid-thought, and just read it to us? And then tell us what you're hearing that we'd miss on the page.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read aloud and model close listening — sets the sensory, embodied register for the whole segment and gives the others something concrete to respond to

questions.question: Eleanor, you'd push back on the word 'incomplete' — you've described the fragmentation in this novel as Eliot's actual method, not a flaw. But here's the devil's advocate: is there a point where you have to admit the seams show? Where the unfinished self tips into just... an unfinished book?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's strongest take on formal fragmentation as deliberate metaphysics, and invite Blackstone to challenge whether 'deliberate mastery' is doing too much work

questions.question: James, Eleanor just made the case that Deronda's crisis is a beautiful formal enactment of modern consciousness. You told me before we started that you find that reading almost dangerously comfortable — that it lets us forget what's actually at stake for him legally and materially. So say the uncomfortable thing: what does it cost us to read this novel as a meditation on art and selfhood rather than as a book about disinheritance?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement between Blackstone and Hartley — Blackstone should articulate the class and legal stakes that a purely formal reading elides; creates the segment's central tension

questions.question: Caroline, James is saying the unfinished self is a legal problem first, a philosophical problem second. But you've argued it's neither — it's embodied, it's gendered, it lives in the body and the voice. How does Gwendolen's version of this crisis feel different from Deronda's? Because they're both unfinished, but they're not unfinished in the same way, are they?
questions.intent: Open the gender dimension — Woodcourt and Blackstone both care about how differently Gwendolen and Deronda experience selfhood, but from different angles; should produce a three-way clash

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you in on this. Eleanor, you said Eliot doesn't write *about* identity, she writes *as* identity. But the novel does end — Deronda sails away, Gwendolen is left on the shore. Does Eliot resolve anything? Or is the forward momentum of sentences, as you put it, just... cut off? And I want James and Caroline to come in after, because I don't think you three agree on what that ending does.
questions.intent: Force a reckoning with the novel's ending as either resolution, abandonment, or deliberate inconclusiveness — all three experts have different positions and this should produce the segment's most heated exchange

steering_notes: This segment has the most potential for genuine three-way tension. The key fault line is between Eleanor's formal-metaphysical reading (fragmentation as mastery), James's materialist reading (fragmentation as legal dispossession), and Caroline's embodied-feminist reading (fragmentation as gendered voice). Don't let any one frame dominate too early. The first question should establish Caroline's close-reading, sensory register so the others have something tactile to push against. The Blackstone-Hartley clash is the engine of the segment — let it run, but use Caroline to redirect toward Gwendolen whenever the conversation threatens to become entirely about Deronda. Save the ending question for last; it forces everyone's hand.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's claim that fragmentation is 'deliberate mastery' directly collides with Blackstone's reading that the unfinished self is a legal condition, not an aesthetic one — push this as soon as Eleanor makes the formal argument

Caroline and Blackstone actually agree that Deronda and Gwendolen experience selfhood differently, but for very different reasons (embodiment vs. class/legal standing) — surface this apparent agreement and then expose the disagreement underneath it

If Eleanor argues that Eliot 'resists resolution,' James will want to point out that Deronda's resolution (Jewish identity, Palestine) is materially specific and historically loaded in ways that aesthetic readings tend to bleach out — flag this as a follow-up opportunity

Caroline's insistence that identity is embodied and happens 'in the voice' sets up a productive complement to Eleanor's syntactic argument — they may be describing the same thing from different angles, and surfacing that could be the segment's most generative moment
